analysis.one_liner: Relieves employers of back taxes for good-faith worker misclassification while forcing disclosure and expanding unemployment coverage.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers sometimes classify workers as independent contractors, so they pay no payroll taxes and the workers get no unemployment insurance or other protections. This bill did two things at once: it made it harder for employers to keep that classification (requiring a genuine, IRS-audit-backed reason, telling the worker what they are losing, and using one uniform federal definition for unemployment programs), and it forgave employers' retroactive tax bills when the misclassification was made in reasonable good faith. It was sent to a House committee and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are actually employees but are labeled contractors would gain the most: the firm paying them would have to tell them, on paper, that they may owe self-employment tax and may be losing unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and workplace protections, and would have to explain how to ask the IRS to review their status. State unemployment systems would gain contributions from newly covered workers. Employers who misclassified workers in reasonable good faith would also gain: their retroactive employment-tax liability would be waived if they signed a monitored agreement to classify similar workers as employees going forward.

how_it_helps.text: Employers who misclassified a worker in reasonable good faith could have their retroactive employment-tax liability waived by signing a closing agreement with Treasury to treat similar workers as employees, with the agreement monitored for at least five years.

Firms paying contractors would have to include on their payment statements that the worker is treated as a non-employee, may owe self-employment tax, is not eligible for fringe benefits, and may lose protections under fair labor standards, health and safety, civil rights, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation laws — plus how to get an IRS review of their status.

The federal safe harbor for treating someone as a non-employee would shrink: an employer would need a reasonable basis, and only a recent IRS employment-tax audit that examined similar positions and approved the treatment would count.
States would have to use a single federal definition of 'employee' for unemployment compensation, closing the gap that lets firms labeled as contractors escape unemployment insurance coverage.
The IRS would regain authority to issue regulations and rulings on employment status, and the special exemption for certain skilled technical personnel would end.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that treat workers as contractors without a reasonable basis would face a harder time defending that treatment against the IRS, and firms in technical fields that previously sat outside the safe harbor entirely would come under it. Treasury would forgo some retroactive tax collections in waiver cases, and businesses signing closing agreements would accept IRS monitoring for five years. Some contractors who prefer non-employee status could find themselves reclassified.

drawbacks.text: The waiver forgives employment taxes (with interest and penalties) for past periods and bars any refund of overpayments, so Treasury would collect less from misclassification cases that it might otherwise have pursued.

Employers signing a closing agreement must treat every substantially similar position as employment and submit to at least five years of Treasury monitoring of wages and contractor payments, a real compliance burden for smaller firms.

Narrowing the safe harbor so that only a recent, targeted IRS audit counts as a reasonable basis removes legal certainty for firms that relied on industry practice or long-standing treatment, raising the cost of using contractors at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a deliberate trade: workers get notice, a way to challenge their status, and stronger unemployment coverage, while good-faith employers get an escape from retroactive tax bills that can be ruinous. The main honest objections are the forgone Treasury collections in waiver cases and the added monitoring burden on compliant employers. Compared with the status quo — workers silently losing benefits and employers facing surprise multi-year back taxes — the design addresses both sides of the problem rather than one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, passed along to its Human Resources subcommittee three weeks later, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Lantos introduced the bill on September 14, 1993, with Rep. Christopher Shays joining as the bill's cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and on September 21, 1993 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Human Resources.
No further action is recorded: the bill sat in committee and never came back to the full House before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors are better off, since they never faced the tightened audit standard, the mandatory worker notices, the end of the technical-personnel exemption, or the uniform unemployment definition. Misclassified workers, meanwhile, kept losing benefits and tax clarity without ever being told.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair, 103rd Congress, was a Democrat)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it sat in the Human Resources subcommittee from September 1993 until the Congress ended, with no markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but no committee or floor votes were ever recorded, so the parties' positions were never tested.

industries.industry: Employers that use independent contractors (courier, trucking, construction, technical services, staffing)
industries.note: These firms would face a tighter safe harbor, mandatory disclosure to their workers, and the loss of the technical-personnel exemption, but good-faith actors would get retroactive liability waived. Their cost is tied to workers' gain: the savings from calling employees contractors come out of the workers' unemployment insurance and labor protections.
A uniform federal definition of employee would bring misclassified workers into covered employment, expanding both benefit access and the contribution base funding the system.

industries.industry: Self-employed and contract workers as a group
industries.note: They would gain notice of their status and an IRS review process, and some would gain employee benefits and unemployment coverage; others could lose the flexibility or tax deductions of non-employee status if reclassified.
